characteristics.cultivar: Ancient wild Camellia sinensis var. assamica (Shan) trees
characteristics.oxidation: 0% (in green style) or partial (for darker styles from the same trees)

description.short: Tea harvested from ancient wild trees growing in misty mountains on the Chinese border, featuring snow-white downy buds and deep forest character
description.overview: Harvested from wild or semi-wild trees, some estimated to be several centuries old — a rare surviving ecosystem of arboreal tea trees thriving naturally in high-mountain cloud forests.
description.leaf: Large plump buds densely covered in white down (hence 'snowy' or tuyết), dark green leaves
description.aroma: Wild mountain forest, raw honey, floral resin
description.taste: Thick, naturally sweet, with woody and forest undertones, far less grassy than plantation tea
description.processing: Hand-harvested from tall wild trees (often requiring ladders) → fixation → rolling → drying

history.origin: The mountainous districts of Ha Giang are primarily inhabited by ethnic minorities (Hmong, Dao, Tay), who have traditionally harvested leaves from ancient wild trees scattered across the forest canopy.
history.development: Some trees in the region are estimated to exceed 300 years of age, standing among the oldest living tea plants on Earth alongside Yunnan's gushu trees.
history.modern: Rising global appreciation for wild-harvested ancient arbor tea has elevated Ha Giang's status as a premium, ecological artisanal tea.
interestingFacts: Northern Vietnam's wild tea forests are botanically contiguous with the ancient tea forests of neighboring Yunnan, China, sharing the evolutionary origins of Camellia sinensis var. assamica.
Harvesting from towering wild trees requires agility and homemade wooden ladders or tree-climbing, demanding intense physical labor compared to manicured plantation rows.
